### Principal component analysis
```{r}
library(stats)

set.seed(123)

keep <- complete.cases(TheCutData[ , -1])  # exclude time column
X <- scale(TheCutData[keep,-1]) #remove time, scale variables

pca <- prcomp(X, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
summary(pca)


pca_var <- pca$sdev^2
pca_var / sum(pca_var)

round(pca$rotation, 2) # loadings (what each PC represents)

biplot(pca, cex = 0.8)

# PCA scores as time series (key step)
scores <- as.data.frame(pca$x)
scores$time <- TheCutData$`Date / time`[keep]

par(mfrow = c(2,1), mar = c(4,4,2,1))

plot(scores$time, scores$PC1, type = "l",
     ylab = "PC1 score", main = "PC1 (Storm-driven mode)")

plot(scores$time, scores$PC2, type = "l",
     ylab = "PC2 score", main = "PC2 (Seasonal mode)")

## plot scores only
# plot(
#   pca$x[, 1],
#   pca$x[, 2],
#   pch = 16,
#   col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.2),
#   xlab = "PC1",
#   ylab = "PC2"
# )     

par(mfrow = c(1,1), mar = c(4,4,2,1))

## plot loadings only
par(mar = c(5, 5, 4, 4) + 0.1)  # bottom, left, top, right margins (in lines)

plot(
  pca$rotation[, 1],
  pca$rotation[, 2],
  type = "n",
  xlab = "PC1",
  ylab = "PC2",
  cex.lab = 1.5,
  cex.axis = 1.3
)

arrows(
  0, 0,
  pca$rotation[, 1],
  pca$rotation[, 2],
  length = 0.1,
  col = "red"
)

text(
  pca$rotation[, 1],
  pca$rotation[, 2],
  labels = rownames(pca$rotation),
  pos = 3,
  cex = 1.3
)
```

### Baseflow separation

```{r}
TheCutDataXTS <- as.xts(TheCutData |> rename(discharge = `Flow at Binfield gauging station (m3/s)`) |> tail(8000) )
TheCutDataXTS$baseflow <- baseflow(TheCutDataXTS$discharge)
TheCutDataXTS$bf_turning <- (TheCutDataXTS$baseflow == TheCutDataXTS$discharge)

# this method gives 1000+ turning points
index(TheCutDataXTS[TheCutDataXTS$bf_turning==1]) |> length()

plot(TheCutDataXTS$discharge, type = "l",
     main = "", main.timespan = FALSE,
     cex.axis = 1.3,
     cex.lab = 1.5)
lines(TheCutDataXTS$baseflow, col = 2, lwd = 2)
abline(v = index(TheCutDataXTS[TheCutDataXTS$bf_turning == 1]), col = "red", lwd = 2)
title(main = expression("Discharge and baseflow (m"^3*"/s)"))

plot(TheCutDataXTS$discharge, type = "l")
lines(TheCutDataXTS$baseflow, col = 2)
abline(a=NULL,b=NULL,h=NULL,v=index(TheCutDataXTS[TheCutDataXTS$bf_turning==1]), col="red")    

median(TheCutDataXTS$baseflow, na.rm=TRUE)
```

Samples rules:
Driven by flow:
1. Baseflow: every week >> sample everything
1. Low flow/algal flush + favourable DO: every day >> sample cholorophyll
1. Track hydrograph: hourly or 3 hourly TP above baseflow (median)
1. High flow for load: track hydrograph like Wong and Kerkez >> 6 points >> TP, assume perfect knowledge of storm coming

```{r}

# 1. Baseflow: every week at 1500>> sample everything

baseline0 <- TheCutData |> 
  mutate(hour = lubridate::hour(`Date / time`), dayofweek = lubridate::wday(`Date / time`)) |> 
  filter(dayofweek==4, hour %in% c(15))


mask_baseline <- TheCutData |>
  mutate(
    hour = lubridate::hour(`Date / time`),
    dayofweek = lubridate::wday(`Date / time`)
  ) |>
  transmute(
    sampled = dayofweek == 4 & hour %in% 15
  ) |>
  pull(sampled)
baseline <- TheCutData[mask_baseline, ]

all.equal(baseline0 |> select(-hour, -dayofweek), baseline)


# 2. Low flow/algal flush + favourable temperature: every day >> sample cholorophyll

criteria <-"(`Flow at Binfield gauging station (m3/s)` < 1.0) & (`Dissolved Oxygen (% saturation)` < 60)"

TheCutData <- flag_event(TheCutData,criteria)

periods  <- extract_event_periods(
   TheCutData %>% 
    rename(timestamp=`Date / time`,flag=event_flag)  |> tidyr::drop_na(flag),
  min_length=5) 

# convert period to R lubridate intervals
intervals <- periods |> 
  mutate(int = lubridate::interval(start,end) ) |> 
  pull(int)


# interval mask (full length of TheCutData)
mask_interval <- Reduce(`|`, lapply(intervals, function(int) TheCutData$`Date / time` %within% int))

# hour mask (full length of TheCutData)
mask_hour <- lubridate::hour(TheCutData$`Date / time`) %in% c(6, 18)

# combined mask — still full length of TheCutData
mask_DO <- mask_interval & mask_hour

rule_low_DO <- TheCutData[mask_DO, ] 

```

1. Track hydrograph: hourly or 3 hourly TP above baseflow (median)


1. High flow for load: track hydrograph like Wong and Kerkez >> 6 points >> TP, assume perfect knowledge of storm coming


```{r above-baseflow}
# 3. Track hydrograph: hourly or 3 hourly TP above baseflow (median)
criteria <-"(`Flow at Binfield gauging station (m3/s)` > 0.122)"

TheCutData <- flag_event(TheCutData,criteria)

periods  <- extract_event_periods(
   TheCutData %>% 
    rename(timestamp=`Date / time`,flag=event_flag)  |> tidyr::drop_na(flag),
  min_length=5) 

# convert period to R lubridate intervals
intervals <- periods |> 
  mutate(int = lubridate::interval(start,end) ) |> 
  pull(int)


# interval mask (full length of TheCutData)
mask_interval <- Reduce(`|`, lapply(intervals, function(int) TheCutData$`Date / time` %within% int))

# hour mask (full length of TheCutData)
mask_hour <- lubridate::hour(TheCutData$`Date / time`) %in% c(0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21)

# combined mask — still full length of TheCutData
mask_HF <- mask_interval & mask_hour

rule_above_baseflow <- TheCutData[mask_HF, ] 
```



### Adaptive sampling using Wong and Kerkez (2016) algorithm
<!-- A real-time probability of precipitation, obtained in our case by querying the public WeatherUndergroundforecast (Weather Underground data from http://www.wunderground.com/), is used to trigger the autosam-pler to take a water quality sample before a storm. This provides a valuable base ﬂow measurement andsafeguards from missing measurements during instances when the hydrograph changes too rapidly or attoo small of an amplitude to be detected by ﬂow sensors alone. The sampling algorithm (Figure 4) uses theweather forecast to trigger a sample when the chance of precipitation exceeding 5 mm within the hour sur-passes 10% (empirically determined based upon an analysis of historical forecasts and the resulting hydro-logic response). Samples are then subsequently triggered based on the estimates of the hydrograph state.While many sampling strategies are possible, in the case of this study, the states of interest included:

 1. base ﬂow conditions right before a storm, 
 2. the onset of the hydrograph to detect a potential ﬁrst ﬂush,
 3. the inﬂection-point of the rising limb of the hydrograph
 4. the peak of the hydrograph 
 5. theinﬂection-point of the falling limb of the hydrograph, 
 6. the falling limb of the hydrograph as it returns to within 10% of the prestorm base ﬂow. 
 
 In the case that the weather forecast is erroneous, the initiation ofa storm event is also marked when the slope in the hydrograph exceeded 7.5 m 3 over 5 min, which for ourstudy site corresponded with the minimum observed change in ﬂow from base ﬂow conditions caused by5 mm of precipitation in 1 h. The algorithm can also be viewed as a state machine, where samples are trig-gered during state transitions, as determined by estimates of the ﬂow x and its derivatives. The statemachine is designed to account for multiple ﬂow regimes (such as delayed surface ﬂows from neighboringslopes), taking additional samples if multiple inﬂection points or local hydrograph peaks are detecte. -->

The Wong and Kerkez (2016, https://doi.org/10.1002/2015WR018013) algorithm uses a state machine to capture six to points in a flow hydrograph.
 1. base ﬂow conditions right before a storm, 
 2. the onset of the hydrograph to detect a potential ﬁrst ﬂush,
 3. the inﬂection-point of the rising limb of the hydrograph
 4. the peak of the hydrograph 
 5. theinﬂection-point of the falling limb of the hydrograph, 
 6. the falling limb of the hydrograph as it returns to within 10% of the prestorm base ﬂow. 

![Adaptive sampling algorithm (above) and corresponding state machine (below) by Wong and Kerkez (2016).](../man/figures/wrcr22370-fig-0004-m.png){.lightbox}


```{r}
RBI = sum(abs(diff(TheCutData$`Flow at Binfield gauging station (m3/s)`)), na.rm=TRUE)/sum(TheCutData$`Flow at Binfield gauging station (m3/s)`, na.rm=TRUE)

print(paste('The Richards-Baker Flashiness Index (RBI) of the station is', RBI))
```

 ```{r}

# parameters
params <- list(
  # forecast_prob_thresh = 0.10,     # 10% POP
  # forecast_rain_thresh = 5,        # mm/hour
  event_frac_thresh <- 0.25,  # 25% above baseflow
  onset_slope_thresh   = 7.5 / 5 /10 ,  # m3/s per min (paper value), may reduce to 0.05
  baseflow_tol_frac    = 0.01,     # 10% of baseflow
  eps                  = 1e-4      # 1e-2 or 1e-6
)

flow_state =  run_state_machine(
    TheCutData$`Date / time`, 
    TheCutData$`Flow at Binfield gauging station (m3/s)`, 
    params = params)

flow_state |> head()

nrow(flow_state)

plot(
  TheCutData$`Date / time`, 
  TheCutData$`Flow at Binfield gauging station (m3/s)`, 
  type = "l",
  xlab = "Time",
  ylab = expression(Discharge~(m^3/s)),
  main = "Hydrograph at the Cut"
)

# abline(h = baseflow, col = "gray", lty = 2)
abline(a=NULL,b=NULL,h=NULL,v=flow_state$time, col="red")    

# very fast!
times = flow_state$time

# subset data by mask, note use %in% for exact time, %within% for intervals
mask_Wong <- Reduce(`|`, lapply(times, function(int) TheCutData$`Date / time` %in% int)) 
rule_state_machine <- TheCutData[mask_Wong, ]
 ```

```{r metrics TP}
raw_col <- "Total Phosphorus (mg/l)"

# reference stats
ref_median <- median(TheCutData[[raw_col]], na.rm = TRUE)
ref_range  <- diff(range(TheCutData[[raw_col]], na.rm = TRUE))
ref_nrows <-  sum(!is.na(TheCutData$`Total Phosphorus (mg/l)`))

combined_TP <- TheCutData |> select(`Date / time`, !!raw_col) |> 
  left_join(baseline |> select(`Date / time`, !!raw_col) |> rename(baseline = !!raw_col) )|> 
  left_join(rule_low_DO |> select(`Date / time`, !!raw_col) |> rename(rule_low_DO = !!raw_col) )|> 
  left_join(rule_above_baseflow |> select(`Date / time`, !!raw_col) |> rename(rule_above_baseflow = !!raw_col) )|> 
  left_join(rule_state_machine |> select(`Date / time`, !!raw_col) |> rename(rule_state_machine = !!raw_col) ) 

metrics_TC <- combined_TP |>
  select(where(is.numeric), -all_of(raw_col)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "series", values_to = "value") |>
  group_by(series) |>
  summarise(
    non_na_count = sum(!is.na(value)),
    median_val       = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    range_val        = diff(range(value, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    pct_median_change = (median_val - ref_median) / ref_median * 100,
    pct_range_change  = range_val / ref_range * 100
  ) |>
  select(series, median_val, non_na_count, pct_range_change, pct_median_change)

metrics_TC |> pivot_longer(series)  |> pivot_wider()
```

## Kolmogorov-Smirnov Tests and `ecdf`
A test to show how good a sub-sampled dataset preseves the characteristics of the orignial one is to overlay their empirical cumulative distribution functions (ecdf). In a perfect scenario, the ecdf of the two time series would completely overlap.

Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests returns the KS statistic, $D$, which is the maximum vertical distance between two cumulative distribution functions (CDFs).

The accompanying p-values tests whether the two time series comes from the same statistical distribution. p-value < 0.05 shows strong evidence that the distrutions differ.
 
 *Caveat:* With very large datasets (common in environmental time series), the KS test becomes extremely sensitive. Even tiny, practically unimportant differences can become statistically significant. In those cases, D is often more informative than the p-value. 

Interpretation guide:
D < 0.05   Very similar
0.05-0.10  Small difference
0.10-0.20  Moderate difference
> 0.20     Large difference


```{r}

## ECDF for TP
pp1 = list(
  `raw data` = TheCutData$`Total Phosphorus (mg/l)`,
  `baseline` = baseline$`Total Phosphorus (mg/l)`,
  `low flow, low DO` = rule_low_DO$`Total Phosphorus (mg/l)`,
  `flow above baseflow` = rule_above_baseflow$`Total Phosphorus (mg/l)`,
  `modified Wong and Kerkez` = rule_state_machine$`Total Phosphorus (mg/l)`
) |> 
  stack() |>  
ggplot(aes(values, colour = ind)) +
  stat_ecdf(linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "Value", y = "ECDF      ", colour = NULL) +
  xlab('Total Phosphorus (mg/L)')+
  guides(
    colour = guide_legend(ncol = 1)
  ) + 
  theme_gov() +
theme(
  legend.text = element_text(lineheight = 0.9, size=20), # add legend space
  legend.position='bottom',
        panel.spacing = unit(2, "lines"),
        text=element_text(size=20), #change font size of all text
        # axis.line = element_line(linewidth = 3, colour = "grey20"),
        strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text=element_text(size=20), #change font size of axis text
        axis.title=element_text(size=20), #change font size of axis titles
        plot.title=element_text(size=16), #change font size of plot title
        legend.title=element_text(size=20)
        ) + 
         scale_colour_manual(
  values = c(
    "raw data" = "black",
    "baseline" = "#0072B2",          # Okabe-Ito blue
```

## extreme statistics
**Extreme Recall**
Extreme Recall measures how many of the truly extreme observations in the full time series were retained after sub-sampling.

Under uniform random sampling:

ExtremeRecallp≈Pr⁡(sampled)\mathrm{ExtremeRecall}_p \approx \Pr(\mathrm{sampled})ExtremeRecallp​≈Pr(sampled)

$$
\mathrm{ExtremeRecall}_p =
\frac{
\#\left(\mathrm{sampled} \cap \{x>P_p\}\right)
}{
\#\left(x>P_p\right)
}
$$

**Oversampling Factor**
If > 1 means, the extremes are X times more frquently sampled than expected under uniform sampling.
$$
\mathrm{OversamplingFactor}_p =
\frac{
\Pr(\mathrm{sampled}\mid x>P_p)
}{
\Pr(\mathrm{sampled})
}
$$

**Tail-Weighted Recall**
It is a ranked-weighted recall that gives more weights to extremes
$$
\mathrm{TailWeightedRecall} =
\frac{
\sum_{i\in S} p_i^{\alpha}
}{
\sum_{i=1}^{N} p_i^{\alpha}
}
$$

**Percentile Exposure**
This is the mean percentile of sampled observations. Complete random sampling should be ¬0.5.
$$
\mathrm{PercentileExposure} =
\frac{1}{|S|}
\sum_{i\in S} p_i
$$

where

$P_p$​ is the ppp-th percentile of the full time series,
$x_i$​ is the value of observation iii,
$N$ is the total number of observations,
$S$ is the set of sampled observations,
$∣S∣$ is the number of sampled observations,
$p_i$​ is the empirical percentile rank of observation iii,
$\alpha$ is the tail-weighting exponent.

```{r extreme}

## need to compare it with full uniform dataset

x = TheCutData$`Total chlorophyll (ug/l)`
sampled_mask = mask_DO

extreme_sampling_metrics(
  full_values = x,
  sampled_mask = sampled_mask,
  percentile = 0.99,
  alpha = 2
)

masks <- list(
  all_data = rep(TRUE,length(mask_baseline)),
  mask_baseline = mask_baseline,
  mask_DO = mask_DO, ## filter timing also
  mask_HF = mask_HF,
  mask_Wong = mask_Wong
)

library(purrr)
library(dplyr)

# show sampling fraction
tibble(
  method = names(masks),
  sampling_fraction = purrr::map_dbl(masks, mean)
)

results <- imap_dfr(
  masks,
  ~ extreme_sampling_metrics(
      full_values = TheCutData$`Total chlorophyll (ug/l)`,
      sampled_mask = .x,
      percentile = 0.99,
      alpha = 2
    ) |>
    mutate(method = .y)
)

results
```
The adaptive sampling scheme perform very well to capture extremes in total chlorophyll *a*. P99 extreme recall shows 34.3% (HF), 9.8% (Wong) and 4.9% (DO) of P99 extremes captured. Tail wegithed recall HF (0.59) and DO (0.16) also shows good performance to retain tail-weighted infromation.

<!-- Baseline and mask_Wong basically picks up no phosphus P99 extremes. As we see in the PDF, the data has a long tail. mask_DO captures 21.3% of all P99 phosphorus observations and 22.3% of overall tail information (if we weighted the data by a factor of $\alpha$ = 2). its oversampling factor is also > 1 meaning it is more likely to sample P99 data than random sampling. mask_HF retains 48% of tail-weghted information. But given it has a high sampling fraction of 64%, this is actually not very good and also explains its low over-sampling factor. -->
